extraction.name: FLEURS: Few-shot Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech
extraction.description: FLEURS is an n-way parallel speech dataset in 102 languages built on top of the machine translation FLoRes-101 benchmark, with approximately 12 hours of speech supervision per language. FLEURS can be used for a variety of speech tasks, including Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification (Speech LangID), Translation and Retrieval.
extraction.creator: Alexis Conneau, Min Ma, Simran Khanuja, Yu Zhang, Vera Axelrod, Siddharth Dalmia, Jason Riesa, Clara Rivera, Ankur Bapna (Meta AI Research, Google Research, Carnegie Mellon University)
extraction.inLanguage: 102 languages including Afrikaans, Amharic, Arabic, Armenian, Assamese, Asturian, Azerbaijani, Belarusian, Bengali, Bosnian, Bulgarian, Burmese, Cantonese Chinese, Catalan, Cebuano, Croatian, Czech, Danish, Dutch, English, Estonian, Filipino, Finnish, French, Fula, Galician, Ganda, Georgian, German, Greek, Gujarati, Hausa, Hebrew, Hindi, Hungarian, Icelandic, Igbo, Indonesian, Irish, Italian, Japanese, Javanese, Kabuverdianu, Kamba, Kannada, Kazakh, Khmer, Korean, Kyrgyz, Lao, Latvian, Lingala, Lithuanian, Luo, Luxembourgish, Macedonian, Malay, Malayalam, Maltese, Mandarin Chinese, Maori, Marathi, Mongolian, Nepali, Northern Sotho, Norwegian, Nyanja, Occitan, Oriya, Oromo, Pashto, Persian, Polish, Portuguese, Punjabi, Romanian, Russian, Serbian, Shona, Sindhi, Slovak, Slovenian, Somali, Sorani Kurdish, Spanish, Swahili, Swedish, Tajik, Tamil, Telugu, Thai, Turkish, Ukrainian, Umbundu, Urdu, Uzbek, Vietnamese, Welsh, Wolof, Xhosa, Yoruba, Zulu
extraction.citeAs: Conneau, A., Ma, M., Khanuja, S., Zhang, Y., Axelrod, V., Dalmia, S., Riesa, J., Rivera, C., & Bapna, A. (2022). FLEURS: Few-shot Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech. arXiv:2205.12446.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Starting from the FLoRes-101 dataset, which contains 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia translated by human translators into 101 languages, the authors used the dev and devtest sets (2009 sentences) and re-split them into train (1509), dev (150) and test (350) sentences. For each sentence in the 102 languages, three recordings were collected from three different native speakers, with a balance in terms of sex ratio of at least 30/70% when possible. Each recording was then evaluated by additional workers to assess whether the recording corresponds to the input sentence; invalid recordings were discarded.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Physical data collection, Manual Human Curator, Self-reporting
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: In the first version of the dataset, about 21.5% of the sentences are missing because none of the three recordings were validated. The authors plan to fill these gaps in future versions of the dataset.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Source sentences come from FLoRes-101, extracted from English Wikipedia and translated into 101 languages by human translators. Speech was recorded by native speakers for each of the 102 languages.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Sentences were split into new train, dev and test sets (1509/150/350 sentences). Three recordings per sentence were collected, evaluated, and invalid recordings discarded. Data was split into train/dev/test with disjoint speakers between train/dev and test with target ratio 7:1:2. All segments are within 30 seconds. Speech sampling rate is 16kHz.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: All recordings are kept as-is, either from quiet or noisy environments, without any data augmentations (e.g. SpecAugment, speed perturbation, simulated reverberation). For text, NFC and FST normalization were applied to each sentence, followed by lower-casing, normalization and removal of punctuation. Words were split into characters, defining the token | as word boundaries. Three versions are provided per sentence: raw transcript (SRC_RAW), preprocessed version (SRC_NORM), and character-based version (SRC_CHAR).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Source transcripts were produced by human translators from FLoRes-101. Speech recordings were collected from three native speakers per sentence. Each recording was then evaluated by additional human workers who assessed whether the recording corresponded to the input sentence; invalid recordings were discarded.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Three recordings per sentence by three different native speakers, followed by validation by additional workers.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Native speakers of each of the 102 languages, with a sex ratio balance of at least 30/70% when possible.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is publicly available via TFDS at https://tensorflow.org/datasets/catalog/xtreme_s and Huggingface at https://hf.co/datasets/google/xtreme_s. The authors plan to fill gaps (missing sentences) in future versions of the dataset.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Speaker sex (sex ratio balance of at least 30/70% was imposed when possible) and language/geographic origin (native speakers of 102 languages).
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The goal of FLEURS is to enable speech technology in more languages and catalyze research in low-resource speech understanding, enabling progress towards building speech technologies for everyone.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Results are much better on Western European languages (average CER 10.7/10.6) than on Sub-Saharan African (15.6/16.4) or South Asian (17.4/19.2) groups, partly due to the larger amounts of unlabeled data in WE languages from MLS and VoxPopuli. Most of the data seen during pre-training is from Western European and Eastern European languages, while CMN, SEA, SSA and SA regions have limited amounts of publicly available pre-training data.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: About 21.5% of sentences are missing in the first version because no recordings were validated. Gaps in performance exist across geographical groups. Some languages are unseen in pre-training, leading to worse fine-tuning performance. CJK languages face tokenization mismatches between fine-tuning and pre-training. Odia's unique script leads to it being unrepresented in some tokenizers. Urdu utterances are sometimes transliterated into Devanagari script, being acoustically similar to Hindi.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: FLEURS is well-suited for several downstream tasks including ASR, Speech-to-Text and Speech-to-Speech Translation, Speech LangID, and Multilingual Speech-to-Speech and Speech-to-Text Retrieval. It can be used for Training, Testing, and Validation, particularly to evaluate data-efficient multilingual pre-trained representations of speech and text, and for few-shot learning evaluation.
